A page not read is marked where it stands, and section 6 counts them. "Opened" means the page answered and its title was read: the pages were not read end to end. For a source whose address is a GitHub repository, the research read the repository's record through the GitHub API (the archived flag, the last push, the licence, the latest release) and not the tool's documentation site. Where a page's title ends with its site's name after a vertical bar or a hyphen, the row gives the part before it. A title is given in quotation marks where the research read one; a source with a name and no quotation marks is one whose title the research does not give.

The research took 64 addresses from the sibling definitions, which opened them on 2026-11-14 or 2026-11-15, and did not fetch them again for their content: the rows give each with its URL as any other. They are, among the sources of this section, from the architects' definition, the SRE book's "Release Engineering", "Service Level Objectives" and "Postmortem Culture", the Workbook's "Canarying Releases" and error budget policy, the two articles of the AWS Builders' Library, Martin Fowler's BlueGreenDeployment, CanaryRelease, ParallelChange and FeatureFlag, DORA's index of capabilities, Semantic Versioning, the three Well-Architected frameworks, AWS's reliability pillar and the CNCF Landscape; from the security team's, the two OWASP cheat sheets, the Twelve-Factor App's Config, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, Doppler, Infisical, 1Password, the CIS Benchmarks, GitHub Actions' "Secure use reference", OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks, SLSA, OpenSSF Scorecard's site, SPDX, CycloneDX, Syft, Docker Scout, Renovate's documentation and Dependabot; from the ETL team's, PostgreSQL's and MySQL's backup pages, RDS's and Cloud SQL's, the SRE book's "Data Integrity", NIST SP 800-34, pgBackRest, Barman and spatie/laravel-backup; from the QA team's, GitLab CI/CD's documentation and the table of contents of Software Engineering at Google; and among the tools of section 4, from the architects' definition, Renovate's and OpenSSF Scorecard's repositories, Jaeger and k6, with OpenTelemetry's home, which no row uses; from the security team's, gitleaks, TruffleHog, Trivy, Checkov, hadolint, zizmor and actionlint.

The address tried was written from memory and answered 403, so the research gives none and this document gives none. CISA's alert page opened; its title was read as far as "CISA and NSA Release Joint Guidance on", and the rest is from the address.

Some names differ from those the user was offered, and the document gives each as its page does:

## 4. Tools the team runs

In an existing project the team runs what the project uses. Each tool runs only where the project's stack takes it. The user took the widest option for each of the eight kinds.

GitLab: the CI lint through glab, "glab ci lint" (https://docs.gitlab.com/cli/ci/lint/), glab itself being at https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli, its licence not read, and gitlab-ci-local (https://github.com/firecow/gitlab-ci-local). Three decisions the user took on 2026-11-15, after the research on the sources and the tools, each the option recommended. The rows above carry them:

- Trivy stays, always at a pinned and verified version (a release's signature or its checksum), and never through `trivy-action` at a moving tag; in CI the action is pinned by SHA. Grype stands beside it as a second reading.
- Tools whose licence is not open (Terraform and Vault, under the Business Source License; Serverless Framework 4; sentry-cli; Docker Scout's CLI): only where the project already uses them under its own licence. The team never installs them, and on a new project it proposes the open alternative (OpenTofu, OpenBao). This is the rule the QA team's definition holds for LocalStack. Serverless Framework stands in section 3 alone, and the rule is said there.
- Stopped tools (Volta, rbac-tool, Overmind): only where the project already uses them. The team installs mise, uses `kubectl auth can-i` and uses process-compose in their place. Volta is no tool of a kind above: it stands in section 3's row "Reproducibility", and the rule is said there. gitleaks stays as on the security team, since it is still patched; Betterleaks is named and not installed.

What the research found of the tools' state on 2026-11-15. "Quiet" means the last release or the last push is older than six months and the repository is not archived:

- Trivy: Aqua's post, last updated on 2026-04-01, says the attacker also force-pushed all 7 tags of `aquasecurity/setup-trivy`, and that malicious Docker Hub images 0.69.5 and 0.69.6 followed on 2026-03-22. The advisory is GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c; safe by the post: Trivy v0.69.2 and v0.69.3, trivy-action v0.35.0, setup-trivy v0.2.6. The CVE number, CVE-2026-33634, rests on a search result. Trivy is under Apache-2.0, v0.76.2 of 2026-11-05.
- Not open source: Terraform (v1.17.2 of 2026-11-11) and Vault (v2.2.2 of 2026-11-12) are under the Business Source License, and their LICENSE files name IBM as the licensor; OpenTofu (v1.13.9 of 2026-11-05) and OpenBao (v2.7.2 of 2026-10-26) are the forks under MPL-2.0, OpenBao a Sandbox project at OpenSSF. Serverless Framework 4: its repository's LICENSE is a link to a "serverless customer agreement", and its README says the npm module holds proprietary software and that providers other than AWS are deprecated; the price terms were not read. sentry-cli is under FSL-1.1-MIT (3.8.2 of 2026-10-22). Docker Scout's CLI is under the Docker Subscription Service Agreement (v1.29.0 of 2026-10-28).
- Unmaintained: Volta, by its own README ("Volta is unmaintained... We recommend migrating to mise"), v2.0.2 of 2024-12-05, last push 2025-11-15, not archived.
- Feature complete: gitleaks, by its own README ("Future releases will be security patches only"), v8.30.1 of 2026-03-21, last push 2026-10-28, MIT. Betterleaks is at `betterleaks/betterleaks`, MIT, v1.10.1 of 2026-11-12.
- Stale and not archived: rbac-tool (v1.20.0 of 2024-10-29, last push 2025-02-13) and Overmind (v2.5.1 of 2024-03-26, last push 2025-04-04).
- Quiet and not archived, the ten the research lists: Foreman (no release, last push 2025-07-27), detect-secrets (v1.5.0 of 2024-05-06), dotenv-linter (v4.0.0 of 2025-10-18, last push 2026-02-05), dive (v0.13.1 of 2025-03-29), dockle (v0.4.15 of 2025-01-06), container-structure-test (v1.22.1 of 2025-12-16), slsa-verifier (v2.7.1 of 2025-06-27), actionlint (v1.7.12 of 2026-03-30), kube-linter (v0.8.3 of 2026-03-10) and yamllint (v1.38.0 of 2026-01-13). The last seven had pushes within six months. Nothing on the list is archived.
- Copyleft licences: TruffleHog, Renovate, Grafana and k6 (AGPL-3.0); hadolint, yamllint, ansible-lint, Ansible and Barman (GPL-3.0); Nix (LGPL-2.1). dockle states its licence two ways: Apache-2.0 in its LICENSE file and in its README's licence section, "AGPL v3" in a badge at the top of its README.
- Repositories that moved: Podman and Buildah from `containers/` to `podman-container-tools/`, Velero from `vmware-tanzu/velero` to `velero-io/velero`, SST from `sst/sst` to `anomalyco/sst`, Sealed Secrets from `bitnami-labs/` to `bitnami/sealed-secrets`, zizmor from `woodruffw/zizmor` to `zizmorcore/zizmor`.
- New major versions since the names were offered: Helm 4, Podman 6, Docker Compose 5, cosign 3, Argo CD 3, Prometheus 3, Grafana 13, Terragrunt 1, SST 4, Serverless Framework 4, sentry-cli 3, datadog-ci 5, pinact 5, Changesets CLI 3, Nuxt 4, and k6 2 and Jaeger 2 by the architects' definition. A project still on Helm 3 runs its own version.
- tfsec is not on the list: its README sends its users to Trivy, so "Trivy config" is the right name.
- Not read: glab's licence; wrangler's and the vercel CLI's own versions; whether git-cliff is offered under MIT too; which schemas check-jsonschema ships.
- Not read on a page: `circleci config validate`, amtool, kubectl's server dry-run flag, `go mod verify` and `cargo --locked`.
- The research gives no page for the comparison of `.env.example` with what the code reads, the secret managers' CLIs, the Makefile and scripts, `kubectl logs`, the platform's log CLI, dashboards and alerts as code, or the cloud's cost CLI; the rows name them with no URL of their own.

## 5. MCP servers and skills

### The rules

1. The other teams' rule: only an MCP server or skills made by a tool's own team. A tool with no server of its own runs from the command line.
2. The server of a tool of point 2 enters only where the project uses the tool, and always reading: OpenTofu's, Terraform's (only where the project already uses Terraform), Prometheus's, Kubecost's, OpenCost's, Infracost's and Ansible AAP's. Argo CD's and Flux's enter with the read-only switch on, as the two exceptions to rule 3, the user's choice and not the option recommended: only where the project already uses them, and only after the building item shows the install command with the switch (`MCP_READ_ONLY=true`; `--read-only`). A server admitted whose reading alone the research did not confirm is not installed until the building item shows that it only reads: Infracost's. Left out: Pulumi's, which can approve changes, Vault's, which returns secret values, and Docker's gateway and Hub servers; those tools run from the command line, only up to the plan.
3. No server that acts on a cloud account, a platform or a cluster enters, with or without a read-only switch: Red Hat's Kubernetes server, AKS's, EKS's, GKE's, the AWS MCP Server and the AWS API server, the Azure MCP Server, gcloud's, Cloud Run's, Cloudflare's API server, Vercel's, Netlify's, Render's, Fly.io's, Railway's, Heroku's, DigitalOcean's. The two exceptions are Argo CD's and Flux's servers, under rule 2. The team reads state through the platform's CLI with read-only credentials and rehearses up to the plan. The reason said to the user: two of the switches are called not guaranteed by their own publishers ("best-effort", "not a security boundary"), and an error here deletes real infrastructure. The clouds' knowledge servers, which serve documentation, stay as on the architects team.
4. The server of a service with an account (CI, delivery, incidents, observability) enters only where the project already uses the service, and always reading: GitHub's and Buildkite's, as on the QA team, Azure DevOps's, Harness's, with `HARNESS_READ_ONLY`, Rootly's, incident.io's, Grafana's, as on the architects team, Sentry's and Datadog's, as on the other teams. A server admitted whose reading alone the research did not confirm is not installed until the building item shows that it only reads: Sentry's. GitHub's is installed without its two secret scanning tools, which return the secret's value by default, the user's decision of 2026-11-16. Left out, as writing with no read-only mode found: GitLab's, CircleCI's, Jenkins's, env0's, Spacelift's, PagerDuty's, Better Stack's, JFrog's (no licence), Vantage's, Octopus's (deprecated).
5. Outside skills: each set only where the project already uses that tool or platform, the rule decided on the QA team, and the skills alone: without the hooks that approve a CLI by themselves (Render's and Railway's plugins) and without the servers that act on the account (the AWS, Azure, Cloudflare and Fly plugins). Skills that publish or approve stay out: HashiCorp's four Packer skills and `pulumi-neo-handoff`. A skill inside an admitted set that deploys, triggers a pipeline, installs on a host or spends enters with its set, the user's choice and not the option recommended; the research names `netlify-deploy`, `azure-deploy`, `render-deploy`, `buildkite-cli`, the `dd-agent-install-*` skills, `aws-agents-for-devsecops` and `fix-findings`. When one of them is used, the rule applies that a deploy to production, and any command that deletes or changes a real resource, is a person's decision. The sets: HashiCorp's, Pulumi's, Flux's, Buildkite's, Infracost's, Render's, Fly's, Railway's, Grafana's, Netlify's, Cloudflare's, Datadog's, Sentry's, Vercel's (vercel-plugin), and the clouds' already on the architects team (the Agent Toolkit for AWS, azure-skills, Google's). With no licence, left out: `vercel-labs/agent-skills`, `docker/claude-plugins`, CircleCI's. Trail of Bits' and Matt Pocock's skills already enter by other definitions.
6. The conflict with two other definitions, decided for all three teams: no server that acts on an account enters by a set of skills or by another team's row. The architects' document is corrected in the same item, on the rows of the Agent Toolkit for AWS and azure-skills and in rule 5: of each the skills alone are installed, where the project is on that cloud, without the server that acts on the account. The security team's document (`docs/specs/2026-11-15-security-team-design.md`) is corrected in the same item: Vault's server and the server of Cloudflare's plugin are left out there as well, and of Cloudflare's plugin only the skills are installed.
7. The team's own skills, seven, defined here and written in a later item: devops (the fifteen subjects as references; the entry); pipelines (the gates before a deploy, jobs that run, pinned actions, the pipeline's supply chain); secrets and identities (where secrets live, least privilege, nothing widened); environment and containers (bringing the project up, health and logs, Dockerfile and images, pinned versions, nothing tied to one machine); infrastructure as code (validate and plan, never apply, policy and the plan's cost); deploy and rollback (the strategy, the release, what undoes each destructive step, backups and the restore rehearsal); operation (logs, metrics, traces, alerts, incidents and runbooks).

The rules stand in the request document's words: its "point 2" is section 4 of this document.

A command that takes a token or a key is written with the variable's name or the page's placeholder and no value. Each row's second cell says where the server runs, whether it can write or act, how reading alone is obtained, its licence, and the label its publisher gives it when it gives one. "Hosted" means the project's data leaves the machine. Where the research of 2026-11-15 gives no command for a row, or none for Claude Code, the fourth cell says so; where it gives no address, the third cell says so. A fact the research took from a search result's summary, and not from an opened page, is said to rest on a search result. For a read-only mode, "not found" means the words "read-only", "readonly" and "read_only" were searched for on the page named and nothing came back; it does not mean the server has none.

Rules 2 and 4 ask for reading always. Of the eighteen servers admitted, the research found a switch on eight: Argo CD's, Flux's, GitHub's, Buildkite's, Azure DevOps's, Harness's, Rootly's and Grafana's. Of those eight, the research gives a command or an address that carries the switch for Buildkite's and Rootly's alone; the other six act by default, and none is installed until the building item shows the command with the switch. Three read alone, with nothing to switch: OpenTofu's, Kubecost's and OpenCost's. Three read by default, and writing is turned on by a flag or a variable that is never set: Terraform's, Prometheus's and Ansible AAP's. incident.io's is read-only by a person's choice at the OAuth approval, and Datadog's by a permission set on Datadog's side. Sentry's is cut by the groups of tools granted, with no proof that the group named reads alone, and on Infracost's no read-only mode was found and whether a tool of it writes was not read: under rules 2 and 4 neither is installed until the building item shows that it only reads. Each row says which, and section 6 holds what the building item settles before an install.

No command the research read names a version: the servers install at a moving one (`argocd-mcp@latest`, `harness-mcp-v2`, `mcp-grafana`, the untagged image `hashicorp/terraform-mcp-server`). Section 6 asks that each be pinned before an install, as Trivy is.

It writes: the token scopes its README asks for include `project:write`, `team:write` and `event:write`. No flag is named read-only. Its tools are grouped in "skills" (`inspect`, `triage`, `seer` and `project-management` are named) that are granted or cut: a group is granted with `--skills=inspect` or `MCP_SKILLS`, and on the hosted address with `?skills=`; a group is cut with `--disable-skills=project-management` or `MCP_DISABLE_SKILLS`. Which group holds which write tool was not read, so that `inspect` alone holds no write tool is not confirmed: under rule 4 the server is not installed until the building item shows that it only reads. Under the "Functional Source License, Version 1.1, Apache 2.0 Future License" (FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0), not open source today. No label was found; an "experimental" plugin channel exists. The research did not read the server again on 2026-11-15, and which of its groups serve monitors, logs and incidents was not checked. The QA team's and the architects' definitions install the same server | https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-mcp | `claude mcp add sentry -- sentry mcp`; the command carries no `--skills=inspect` |
| Datadog | Datadog's server, hosted, one address per Datadog site (US1: `https://mcp.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp`), with no local stdio option on its page. It writes (`create_datadog_monitor` is named). No switch per connection: reading alone is by Datadog's permission `mcp_read`, a write needing `mcp_write`, and an administrator disables MCP Write Access or removes scopes from the client's OAuth app. So reading is set on Datadog's side, by a person, and not by anything the install writes. Toolsets are chosen with `?toolsets=`; which toolsets serve monitors, logs and incidents was not read. Its repository is MIT by the QA team's definition; the research of 2026-11-15 names no licence for the hosted service. The research did not read the server again on 2026-11-15. The QA team's and the architects' definitions install the same server | https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ | `claude mcp add --transport http datadog https://mcp.datadoghq.com/v1/mcp`; no toolset is in the command |

The team reads a CI the project has and that this table does not name from the command line, with gh, glab, the circleci CLI or bk (section 4).

### Left out

Left out by rule 2, their tools running from the command line, only up to the plan:

- Pulumi's server (https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/guides/ai-integration/mcp-server/): hosted only, at `https://mcp.ai.pulumi.com/mcp`; no public repository was found. The page says the server never runs `pulumi up`, and it reads Pulumi Cloud. It acts through `neo-bridge`, which starts Neo tasks and sends approvals: an approval "can let Neo change infrastructure or open pull requests". No read-only mode is documented; the page's two controls are an organisation token with a restricted role, which "doesn't block Neo tasks", and denying `mcp__pulumi__neo-bridge` in Claude Code's `permissions.deny`. The page states no licence and no label.
- HashiCorp Vault's server (https://github.com/hashicorp/vault-mcp-server), MPL-2.0, on the machine, "intended for local use only" by the security team's definition: `create_mount`, `delete_mount`, `write_secret`, `delete_secret`, the PKI tools, and `read_secret`, by which the secret's value reaches the model. No read-only mode was found; the only limit is the Vault token's policy. The security team's definition, corrected under rule 6 in the same item, leaves it out as well.
- Docker's MCP Gateway (https://github.com/docker/mcp-gateway), MIT, with the Toolkit, whose page the QA team's definition opened and the research did not open again (https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-catalog-and-toolkit/toolkit/): a gateway and catalogue that runs other MCP servers as containers, and not a server for Docker itself. Tools are cut per profile; no read-only mode was found in its README, whose lines on Claude Code were not read.
- Docker Hub's server (https://github.com/docker/hub-mcp, and its page at https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-catalog-and-toolkit/hub-mcp/), Apache-2.0, on the machine, calling Docker Hub's API with `HUB_PAT_TOKEN`: it writes (`create-repository`, `set-repository-dockerfile`, `update-repository-info`), no delete tool being listed. No read-only mode was found on the page or in the README.

Left out by rule 3, each a server that acts on a cloud account, a platform or a cluster, with or without a read-only switch:

- Red Hat's Kubernetes server (https://github.com/containers/kubernetes-mcp-server), of the `containers` organisation and not of the Kubernetes project, Apache-2.0, on the machine with the kubeconfig: "Any CRUD operation (Create or Update, Get, List, Delete)" on any resource, it deletes pods, runs "Exec into a pod and run a command", runs an image, and has a `helm` toolset. Read-only with `read_only = true` in a TOML file passed with `--config`, the flag `--read-only` being "no longer accepted". Its README calls `read_only` and `denied_resources` "best-effort guardrails" and says Kubernetes RBAC is "the access control to rely on".
- AKS's server (https://github.com/Azure/aks-mcp), Microsoft's, MIT, on the machine only: it runs `az`, `kubectl`, `helm`, `cilium` and `hubble` "using the identity of the process it runs as". `--access-level` is `readonly` by default, with `readwrite` and `admin`; in `readwrite` it creates, deletes, scales, starts and stops clusters. Its README calls `--access-level` "a guardrail to reduce accidental damage" and says it is not a security boundary against a deliberately malicious caller: "Treat the ability to call AKS-MCP as equivalent to handing over a shell".
- EKS's servers. The local one, of AWS Labs (`src/eks-mcp-server` in https://github.com/awslabs/mcp, Apache-2.0), reads by default; `--allow-write` enables "create, update, delete" (`apply_yaml`, `manage_k8s_resource`, `manage_eks_stacks`, `add_inline_policy`), and `--allow-sensitive-data-access` opens logs, events and secrets. The hosted one, for EKS and ECS, is known by a search result alone, its page being https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/eks-mcp-introduction.html (not opened): "in preview release", with read-only and full-access managed policies, and no server-level read-only mode found in the summary.
- GKE's server (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/gke-mcp), Apache-2.0, on the machine, "not an officially supported Google product", "This software is experimental": `create_cluster`, `update_cluster`, `delete_cluster` "(if enabled)", node pools, `gke_deploy`, `apply_k8s_manifest`, `delete_k8s_resource`. No read-only mode was found, nor what "if enabled" is switched by.
- The AWS MCP Server (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html), the hosted one of the Agent Toolkit for AWS, one address per Region: `aws___run_script` ("Execute Python code in a sandboxed environment with AWS API access") and `aws___get_presigned_url`, with "Full AWS API coverage". Read-only with SigV4, by the flag `--read-only` of the local proxy (https://github.com/aws/mcp-proxy-for-aws: "Disable tools which may require write permissions"), or by IAM condition keys, whose names were not read; with OAuth no read-only switch was found. The toolkit's README badge says "status-GA", and the `awslabs/mcp` README still writes "AWS MCP Server (in preview)".
- The AWS API server (`src/aws-api-mcp-server` in https://github.com/awslabs/mcp), of AWS Labs, on the machine: it runs any AWS CLI command with the credentials' rights. Read-only with `READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY=true` ("restricts execution to read-only operations only"); `REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT=true` asks before a mutation. It warns that read operations "can still return AWS credentials or sensitive information", its telemetry to AWS is on by default, and at start it shows a deprecation notice that "recommends migrating to the AWS MCP Server".
- The Azure MCP Server (https://github.com/microsoft/mcp), Microsoft's, MIT, on the machine with the signed-in Azure identity, "now generally available" at 2.0: "Autonomous or misconfigured clients may perform destructive actions". A read-only mode exists, shown as the VS Code setting `"azureMcp.readOnly"`; the command-line flag's name was not read.
- gcloud's server (https://github.com/googleapis/gcloud-mcp), Google's, Apache-2.0, on the machine, "currently in preview" and "not an officially supported Google product": `run_gcloud_command` "Executes a gcloud command", so anything the account may do, minus a deny list. No read-only mode was found; the README's control is a service account with a limited role.
- Cloud Run's server (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/cloud-run-mcp), Google's, Apache-2.0: `deploy-file-contents`, `deploy-local-folder` and `create-project` ("Creates a new GCP project and attach it to the first available billing account"). No read-only mode was found.
- Cloudflare's API server (https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp), Apache-2.0, hosted at `https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp`: `execute` runs JavaScript that calls `cloudflare.request()` over "2500 endpoints". No mode is named read-only; reading alone is by the permissions chosen at the OAuth consent or by an API token created with read permissions.
- Vercel's server (https://vercel.com/docs/agent-resources/vercel-mcp), hosted at `https://mcp.vercel.com`: "manage projects and deployments", a changelog entry titled "Vercel MCP can now deploy code", and it "grants the AI system you're using the same access as your Vercel user account". No read-only mode was found on the two pages read; a guide on "read-only access to deployment data through Vercel Connect" was not opened. The page states no licence.
- Netlify's server (https://github.com/netlify/netlify-mcp, and its page at https://docs.netlify.com/welcome/build-with-ai/netlify-mcp-server/), hosted at `https://mcp.netlify.com/mcp` or on the machine, with no licence: "Create, manage, and deploy Netlify projects", "Modify access controls", "Create and manage environment variables and secrets". No read-only mode was found in the README or on the page.
- Render's server (https://github.com/render-oss/render-mcp-server, and its page at https://render.com/docs/mcp-server), Apache-2.0: it creates web services, static sites, cron jobs, Postgres and Key Value instances, replaces environment variables, triggers deploys, and `approve_blueprint` applies a planned sync; it cannot delete resources. The page warns it "supports potentially destructive operations". No read-only mode was found.
- Fly.io's server (https://docs.fly.io/flyctl/mcp-server), inside flyctl, labelled "[experimental] Start a flyctl MCP server": the page documents start-up options only, and what the server can do was not on it. Fly's own plugin guard names MCP tools that delete, exec, set secrets and create billable resources. No read-only mode was found.
- Railway's server (https://docs.railway.com/cli/mcp), inside the Railway CLI, or hosted at `https://mcp.railway.com`: the tools and what writes are not on the page, and no read-only mode was found. The older npm package and `railwayapp/railway-mcp-server` are deprecated and archived.
- Heroku's server (https://github.com/heroku/heroku-mcp-server), Apache-2.0, on the machine through the Heroku CLI: `create_app`, `deploy_to_heroku`, `deploy_one_off_dyno`, `ps_scale`, `create_addon`, which provisions a paid add-on, `pipelines_promote`, `pg_psql`, which runs SQL. No read-only mode was found.
- DigitalOcean's server (https://github.com/digitalocean-labs/mcp-digitalocean), MIT, hosted at `https://mcp.digitalocean.com/mcp` with one address per service: "Create, manage, resize, snapshot" droplets, "Provision" databases, Kubernetes clusters and node pools, App Platform deployments. No read-only mode was found.

The research read more servers that rule 3's sentence covers and its list does not name; none enters. Google Cloud's managed remote servers (https://docs.cloud.google.com/mcp/overview and https://docs.cloud.google.com/mcp/supported-products): each product's tools were not read, and no read-only mode was found on the two pages. AWS Labs' further servers in `awslabs/mcp`: ECS's (it builds and pushes images and deletes; `ALLOW_WRITE=false` and `ALLOW_SENSITIVE_DATA=false`), Serverless's ("runs in read-only mode by default"; `--allow-write`), Finch's, and the IaC server, which validates templates and where no deploy tool was read. Cloudflare's product servers (https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp-server-cloudflare), ten of them under "Deprecated servers. Please migrate to the Cloudflare API MCP Server". Azure DevOps's local server and Octopus's stand under rule 4.

The clouds' knowledge servers stay as on the architects team (`docs/specs/2026-11-15-architects-team-design.md`, section 5, "Knowledge servers, where the project is on that cloud"): the AWS Knowledge MCP Server, the Microsoft Learn MCP Server, Google's Developer Knowledge server and Cloudflare's Documentation server. The research notes that the AWS page now recommends removing the AWS Knowledge MCP Server in favour of the AWS MCP Server.

Left out by rule 4, the servers of services with an account. The rule gives them as writing with no read-only mode found; the lines say what the research states of each:

- GitLab's server (its tools reference at https://docs.gitlab.com/user/gitlab_duo/model_context_protocol/mcp_server_tools/, of which the first 100,000 of 136,190 characters were read): on the project's GitLab instance, "Generally available" since GitLab 19.5 by the QA team's definition. Its `ci` toolset reads with `get_pipeline`, `get_job`, `get_artifact_file`, `list_pipelines` and `list_pipeline_schedules`, and acts with `save_pipeline`, which creates, retries or cancels a pipeline, and the unlisted `manage_pipeline`, which deletes. No read-only mode was found in the part read; how a toolset is switched was not read.
- CircleCI's server: hosted, `rerun_workflow` and `cancel_workflow` act, and its page gives no read-only mode, by the QA team's definition; the research did not read it again and gives no address.
- Jenkins's server (https://github.com/jenkinsci/mcp-server-plugin), a plugin of the Jenkins project, MIT, inside the project's Jenkins: `triggerBuild`, `rebuildBuild`, `replayBuild` ("Run a Pipeline build again with a modified script"). No read-only mode was found; access follows the Jenkins user's permissions.
- env0's server (https://github.com/env0/mcp-server), "Envzero's official MCP server", Apache-2.0: `deploy-environment`, `abort-environment`, `cancel-environment`, and `approve-environment` ("Approve an environment plan, pending approval for applying"), which applies real infrastructure. No read-only mode was found.
- Spacelift's server (https://github.com/spacelift-io/spacectl), inside `spacectl`, MIT: the tools and what writes were not read, and no read-only mode was found.
- PagerDuty's server (https://docs.pagerduty.com/ai-automation/advance/pagerduty-mcp-server), hosted: the `manage_*` tools create and update incidents, add notes and responders, start workflows and change services, schedules and teams. No read-only mode was found for the hosted server ("Tool filtering isn't directly available"); the page's control is a Scoped OAuth client. The local repository is archived.
- Better Stack's server (https://betterstack.com/docs/getting-started/integrations/mcp/), hosted: it creates, acknowledges, escalates and resolves incidents, changes monitors and status pages, invites and removes team members. No single read-only switch was found; the headers `X-MCP-Tools-Only` and `X-MCP-Tools-Except` cut tools.
- JFrog's server (https://github.com/jfrog/jfrog-mcp-server), "generally available (GA)" on JFrog Cloud, the API showing no licence: "Create and view projects, repositories, and other JFrog components". No read-only mode was found in the lines read; `TOOLS.md` was not opened.
- Vantage's server (https://github.com/vantage-sh/vantage-mcp-server), MIT, hosted or self-hosted: "MCP Server to fetch costs and usage data". Its README speaks of "the corresponding write permissions" for a token; which tools write was not read, and no read-only mode was found.
- Octopus Deploy's server. The local one (https://github.com/OctopusDeploy/mcp-server), MPL-2.0, is marked "Deprecated"; it "runs with write tools enabled by default" and has a flag `--read-only`. The remote one (https://octopus.com/docs/octopus-ai/mcp/remote), on the project's Octopus instance, writes with a command tool, and no read-only mode was found on its page.

The research read further servers that no rule names, and none is installed by this definition: Atlassian's, for Bitbucket with Jira and Confluence (https://github.com/atlassian/atlassian-mcp-server), with no switch per connection found; Honeycomb's and New Relic's, which the architects' definition holds; Checkly's, which the QA team's holds; Infisical's and Trivy's, which the security team's installs, Infisical's with its values masked and Trivy's (https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy-mcp) having no push since 2025-12-17; Doppler's, 1Password's and Snyk's, which the security team's leaves out, as it does Vault's; Jaeger's, OpenSSF Scorecard's and k6's, which the architects' definition holds or leaves out; HashiCorp Consul's (https://github.com/hashicorp/consul-mcp-server), under the Business Source License; Elastic's (https://github.com/elastic/mcp-server-elasticsearch), whose README was not read; Backstage's backend plugin (https://github.com/backstage/backstage), not read. Chainguard's servers and Port's rest on a search result alone, their pages being https://www.chainguard.dev/docs/platform/mcp-servers (not opened) and https://docs.port.io/ai-interfaces/port-mcp-server/installation (not opened).

Skills left out for having no licence, under rule 5:

- `vercel-labs/agent-skills` (https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills): the API shows no licence and the root has no LICENSE file. Nine skills, among them `deploy-to-vercel`, which deploys.
- `docker/claude-plugins` (https://github.com/docker/claude-plugins): the API shows no licence. One plugin, `docker-mcp-toolkit`, and one skill, `mcp-server-yaml-creator`, on writing a catalogue entry for an MCP server and not on Dockerfiles or images.
- CircleCI's skills (https://github.com/CircleCI-Public/skills): still no licence. Fourteen skills. The QA team's definition leaves them out for the same reason.

Skills that publish or approve, left out under rule 5. No other skill of an admitted set is left out: one that deploys, triggers a pipeline, installs on a host or spends enters with its set, and its row names it:

- HashiCorp's four Packer skills, `aws-ami-builder`, `azure-image-builder`, `push-to-registry` and `windows-builder`: they build cloud images and push to a registry, outside "no push to a registry".
- Pulumi's `pulumi-neo-handoff`: it hands work to Neo, Pulumi's hosted agent, which can change infrastructure.

The hooks and the servers the plugins bring, left out under rule 5:

- Render's hook, `hooks/auto-approve-render.sh`, opened in part: it auto-approves single `render ...` Bash commands with plain characters, and exits without approving when the command contains delete, remove, restart, create, deploy, update, set, suspend, resume, scale, stop, start, rollback, promote or cancel. The rest of the hook was not read.
- Railway's hook, `plugins/railway/hooks/auto-approve-api.sh`, opened in part: "Auto-approve railway-api.sh and railway CLI commands". Whether it leaves out deploys, deletes and variable changes was not read.
- The AWS plugin `aws-core`, which "bundles the AWS MCP Server configuration"; the Azure plugin, which "packages the Azure MCP Server"; Cloudflare's plugin, which also configures the hosted `cloudflare` server; Fly's plugin, which ships a `fly` MCP server whose tools delete, exec and create billable resources.
- Fly's hook, `plugins/fly/scripts/fly_guard.py`, asks before risky calls and approves nothing by itself ("The hook is a reminder, not a sandbox"); it comes with the plugin and is not installed with the skills alone.

The research found further sets that rule 5 does not name, and no rule installs them: `getsentry/sentry-for-ai` (https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-for-ai), MIT, 34 skills; AWS Labs' `awslabs/agent-plugins`, Apache-2.0, 34 skills, whose files were not opened; Atlassian's 21 SKILL.md files inside its server's repository, their names not read.

### The team's own skills

Seven skills, defined here and written in a later item.

| Skill | What it does |
| :- | :- |
| DevOps | The entry: the fifteen subjects of section 3 as references |
| Pipelines | The gates before a deploy, jobs that run, pinned actions, the pipeline's supply chain |
| Secrets and identities | Where secrets live, least privilege, nothing widened |
| Environment and containers | Bringing the project up, health and logs, the Dockerfile and images, pinned versions, nothing tied to one machine |
| Infrastructure as code | Validate and plan, never apply; policy and the plan's cost |
| Deploy and rollback | The strategy, the release, what undoes each destructive step, backups and the restore rehearsal |
| Operation | Logs, metrics, traces, alerts, incidents and runbooks |

### Nothing of their own

No server of their own team was found on 2026-11-15 for these, which run from the command line. Only what the research checked stands here, with the check done; it is one check each unless the line says otherwise, and none proves that nothing exists elsewhere:

- The Kubernetes project: a search of the `kubernetes` and `kubernetes-sigs` GitHub organisations for "mcp" in a repository's name returned only `kubernetes-sigs/mcp-lifecycle-operator`, an operator that deploys MCP servers; a web search's summary says the same. The servers that exist are Red Hat's, Google's, AWS's and Microsoft's, all under "Left out".
- Helm: a search of the `helm` organisation, nothing; a web search returned community servers only.
- Hetzner: a search of the `hetznercloud` organisation, nothing; a web search returned third-party servers only.
- Laravel Forge and Laravel Cloud: `laravel/forge-mcp` and `laravel/cloud-mcp` answer 404; a search of the `laravel` organisation returns only `laravel/mcp`, a package for building servers; a web search on Forge returned community servers only. Laravel's own Forge and Cloud documentation was not opened.
- OpenTelemetry: a search of the `open-telemetry` organisation, nothing; a web search returned vendors' servers only.
- Sigstore, and cosign with it: a search of the `sigstore` organisation, nothing; a web search returned nothing.
- Opsgenie: a search of the `opsgenie` organisation, nothing. Atlassian's pages on Opsgenie were not opened.
- Renovate: a search of the `renovatebot` organisation, nothing, as the architects' definition says.
- SOPS (`getsops`), Anchore (`anchore`), for Syft and Grype, and `prometheus-community`: organisation searches, nothing. Anchore's `grype-mcp` was archived on 2026-03-24, by the security team's definition.
- From the security team's definition, not checked again: gitleaks, TruffleHog, Checkov, hadolint, zizmor, Docker Scout and Syft.

No skills of their own team were found where the research looked: `argoproj-labs/agent-skills`, `docker/agent-skills`, `PagerDuty/skills`, `aquasecurity/skills` and `sigstore/skills` answer 404; `gitlab-org/skills` answers 404 on GitHub, GitLab's own host not being searched; Harness's server repository holds no SKILL.md.

The research did not check these tools of section 4 at all, for a server or for skills of their own: actionlint, act, pinact, glab, gitlab-ci-local, yamllint, check-jsonschema, detect-secrets, age, dotenv-linter, rbac-tool, dive, dockle, container-structure-test, Podman, Buildah, tflint, terraform-docs, Terragrunt, Conftest and OPA, cfn-lint, Bicep, ansible-lint, Kustomize, kubeconform, kube-linter, the Dev Containers CLI, mise, asdf, kind, k3d, Tilt, Skaffold, release-please, semantic-release, Changesets, GoReleaser, git-cliff, commitlint, Kamal, stern, cosign and slsa-verifier beyond the search of the Sigstore organisation, restic, pgBackRest, Barman, Velero, spatie/laravel-backup, Overmind and process-compose; nor Coolify and Dokku, of section 3.
